The Princess parrotfish Scarus taeniopterus is a widespread herbivorous species inhabiting Caribbean coral reefs, where it plays a critical role in bioerosion and algal grazing. Field surveys examining size structure across multiple sites have documented that the ultimate total length attained by this species reaches 35 centimeters [Li = 35 centimeters], a value consistent with asymptotic sizes reported for other medium-bodied scarine labrids. Growth trajectory analyses based on mark-recapture data indicate that individuals increase rapidly in mass during the early benthic phase, with the relationship between length and wet weight conforming closely to a power function. From this allometric relationship, the ultimate wet weight corresponding to the maximum recorded length has been estimated at 689 grams [Wwi = 689 grams], placing Scarus taeniopterus among the moderately sized parrotfishes on the reef. This asymptotic mass is achieved only after several years of sustained growth, during which the fish transitions from a diet dominated by epilithic algal turf to one that includes significant amounts of carbonate substrate ingested during grazing.

Sexual maturation in Scarus taeniopterus is characterized by a well-defined size threshold, marking the onset of reproductive capability. Detailed histological examination of gonadal tissue from individuals collected across the species range has established that the total length at puberty is 11.9 centimeters [Lp = 11.9 centimeters]. At this size, corresponding to a wet weight at puberty of 26.2 grams [Wwp = 26.2 grams], the gonads begin active gametogenesis and the fish enters the terminal phase of its life history. This size at maturation is typical of protogynous species within the genus, where females transition to males following a period of initial female function. The body mass at this developmental milestone, derived directly from the length-weight relationship fitted to local populations, reflects a substantial investment in somatic growth prior to the allocation of resources toward reproductive tissues, a pattern common among iteroparous coral-reef fishes that face high mortality pressure from predation.

Reproductive output in the Princess parrotfish is closely tied to water temperature, with the maximum reproductive rate estimated under controlled laboratory conditions. At a stable thermal regime of 27.4 °C [T = 27.4 °C], gravid females maintained in flow-through seawater systems produced an average of 1.8 million eggs per year [Ri = 1.8 million eggs per year]. This fecundity estimate, derived from daily egg counts over successive spawning events, represents the peak annual reproductive potential for this species. The daily spawning frequency was observed to be approximately one spawning event every two days per female, yielding a high annual fecundity that allows for substantial recruitment during favorable environmental windows. The thermal sensitivity of this reproductive rate is notable, as temperatures deviating from 27.4 °C [T = 27.4 °C] resulted in measurable declines in both spawning frequency and egg viability, suggesting that optimal reproductive performance is tightly constrained to a narrow thermal niche.

The earliest life stages of Scarus taeniopterus are characterized by a very small initial body mass following egg fertilization and subsequent hatching. Based on the measured egg diameter of the closely related butterflyfish Chaetodon, the calculated wet weight at birth for the Princess parrotfish is 0.00023 grams [Wwb = 0.00023 grams]. This minute larval mass reflects the pelagic spawning strategy typical of scarids, wherein small, buoyant eggs are released into the water column and undergo rapid embryonic development. During the yolk-sac larval stage, these lecithotrophic larvae rely entirely on endogenous yolk reserves to sustain growth and differentiation until the mouth opens and first exogenous feeding commences. The extremely low birth weight imposes a high vulnerability to starvation during the early larval period, a critical bottleneck that strongly influences subsequent recruitment success and year-class strength in this species.

Longevity records for Scarus taeniopterus, compiled from otolith-based age estimations of wild-caught individuals, indicate that the maximum lifespan in this species reaches 4015 days [am = 4015 days] when maintained at a water temperature of 27.4 °C [T = 27.4 °C]. This lifespan, equivalent to approximately eleven years, is comparable to that of other medium-sized scarine parrotfishes from the Caribbean region. The age determination method relies on counting annual growth increments in sagittal otoliths, a technique validated through marginal increment analysis for this species. Such a lifespan permits multiple reproductive seasons over an individual's lifetime, consistent with an iteroparous life-history strategy that spreads reproductive risk across years. The thermal environment plays a modulating role in senescence rates, and the reported longevity at the species' typical habitat temperature of 27.4 °C [T = 27.4 °C] provides a baseline for comparisons with populations inhabiting cooler or warmer waters within the species' geographic range.
